title: You Think Your Body Borders Are Fixed, Yet Two Paintbrushes Move Your Hand in Seconds
description:
Behavioral & Circuit Analysis — Botvinick & Cohen (1998): Two Paintbrushes, One Fake Rubber Hand & Rewriting Where 'You' End in 60 Seconds, grounded in Matthew Botvinick, Jonathan Cohen (1998) (Nature). Empirical findings show that nothing feels more solid and unchangeable than knowing which flesh-and-bone limbs belong to your own body — until Matthew Botvinick and Jonathan Cohen sat 10 volunteers at a table in 1998 (Nature) with a vertical partition hiding their real left hand while a lifelike prosthetic rubber left hand sat right in plain view.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how somatosensory cortex, premotor cortex, insula coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that for 10 minutes (and in later studies, as little as 45 to 60 seconds!), the experimenter used two identical small paintbrushes to stroke the visible rubber fingers and the hidden real fingers in exact millisecond synchrony.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Matthew Botvinick, Jonathan Cohen (1998). Rubber hands ‘feel’ touch that eyes see. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/35784
- Manos Tsakiris, Patrick Haggard (2005). The Rubber Hand Illusion Revisited: Visuotactile Integration and Self-Attribution. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance. https://doi.org/10.1037/0096-1523.31.1.80
- Marieke Rohde, Massimiliano Di Luca, Marc O. Ernst (2011). The Rubber Hand Illusion: Feeling of Ownership and Proprioceptive Drift Do Not Go Hand in Hand. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0021659

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
